checks.claim: Key: Fe, Au, Ag and Pb come from the elements' Latin names (ferrum, aurum, argentum, plumbum)
checks.note: Wikipedia's table: Fe from Latin ferrum, Au from aurum, Ag from argentum, Pb from plumbum. Grokipedia Chemical_symbol confirms Fe (ferrum) and Au (aurum).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Greek names
checks.note: None of the four symbols comes from Greek; all four are from Latin.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: names of discoverers / places found
checks.note: Berzelius's table gives Ferrum, Aurum, Argentum, Plumbum as the basis; these four metals were known in antiquity, no discoverer or place.

checks.claim: Context: H for hydrogen and O for oxygen come straight from the name
Context: plumbum is the root of the word plumbing
checks.note: Plumbing from Latin plumbum, lead, as early pipes were lead.

checks.claim: Context: the symbols were built from Latin names so that the same letters stand for each element in every language
checks.note: Grokipedia: Berzelius's symbols were 'derived primarily from the Latin names of elements to ensure consistency across languages'. Berzelius's own surviving words (vanderkrogt) give only ease of writing and printing as his reason for letters, so the intent is Grokipedia's reading rather than his stated aim; the effect (same letters in every language) is true. Optional softening: 'Because the symbols were built from Latin, the shared language of scholars, the same letters stand for each element in every language.'

checks.claim: Context: einsteinium (Es) named after Albert Einstein; americium (Am) after the Americas
checks.note: Es for einsteinium, named for Albert Einstein; Am for americium, named after the Americas (by analogy with europium).

checks.claim: Key: hammering gold into thin leaf is malleability
checks.note: Wikipedia: malleability is deformation under compression (historically, forming 'by hammering or rolling'); ductility is plastic deformation 'when undergoing tension'. Grokipedia Gold_leaf: the goldbeating process 'relies on the metal's exceptional malleability'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Ductility (is it partly right?)
checks.note: Grokipedia Gold_leaf's overview loosely credits 'high ductility', but by the standard definitions (ductility = under tension, drawn into wire; malleability = under compression, hammered into sheets) hammering into leaf is malleability. Wikipedia: 'Gold is the most malleable metal, while platinum is the most ductile of the pure metals.' The stem's 'hammers' makes Malleability the only right answer at grade level.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: Lustre, Conductivity
checks.note: Shine and carrying heat/electricity have nothing to do with spreading without cracking.

checks.claim: Stem: gold leaf so thin that light shines through it
checks.note: Wikipedia Gold: 'Gold leaf can be beaten thin enough to become semi-transparent'; Grokipedia Gold_leaf: about 0.1 to 0.2 micrometres, 'translucent'.

checks.claim: Context: gold is the most malleable metal of all
checks.note: 'Gold is the most malleable metal.' Grokipedia Gold agrees.

checks.claim: Context: one gram can be beaten into a sheet of about one square metre
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a sheet covering approximately one square meter'; Wikipedia Gold: 'A single gram of gold can be beaten into a sheet of 1 square meter'.

checks.claim: Context: ductility = drawn into wire, lustre = shine, conductivity = carries heat and electricity
Key: metals fill most of the table, from the left across the middle
checks.note: Grokipedia: metals are 'the vast majority of the 118 known elements (about 94)', about 80%, and 'occupy the left and central regions of the table'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: about half down the left; about half down the right; a small part in the top right
checks.note: Metals are about four in five, not half; the top right corner is where the nonmetals sit ('upper right portion').

checks.claim: Context: about four in five elements are metals
checks.note: Grokipedia about 94 of 118 (about 80%); Wikipedia puts nonmetals at about 15-20% of the 118 elements.

checks.claim: Context: the two rows printed below the table are metals too
checks.note: The lanthanides and actinides (the f-block rows) are all metals; Grokipedia places metals mainly in the s-, d- and f-blocks.

checks.claim: Context: nonmetals in the top right, hydrogen at the top left; metalloids along the staircase line
checks.note: Grokipedia Nonmetal: hydrogen is 'generally classified as a nonmetal despite its group 1 placement'; Grokipedia Metalloid: a 'diagonal staircase band that separates the metals on the left from the nonmetals on the right'.

checks.claim: Stem: germanium is a metalloid with a grey metallic shine
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a gray-white metalloid', pure germanium 'retains a metallic luster in air'. Wikipedia Metalloid: 'a shiny grey-white solid'.

checks.claim: Key: struck hard with a hammer, it shatters into pieces (brittle)
checks.note: Grokipedia: pure germanium 'is crystalline, brittle'; Wikipedia Metalloid: 'hard and brittle'. A brittle crystalline solid breaks under a hard blow rather than deforming.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: flattens into a sheet; bends but does not break; dents but holds together
checks.note: Metalloids 'are brittle rather than malleable or ductile'; all three wrong choices describe malleable or ductile behaviour.

checks.claim: Context: metalloids usually look like metals but behave largely like nonmetals
checks.note: Exact Wikipedia wording; not in quotation marks in the draft.

checks.claim: Context: the same blow would flatten a lump of gold or lead
checks.note: Gold is the most malleable metal; lead is soft and malleable.

checks.claim: Context: silicon has a metallic shine and is brittle
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'a crystalline solid with a blue-grey metallic lustre ... hard and brittle'.

checks.claim: Stem: eleven elements are gases at room temperature, oxygen, nitrogen, chlorine and helium among them
checks.note: Grokipedia: of the 17 nonmetals '11 exist as gases' (hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, chlorine and the noble gases).

checks.claim: Key: every element that is a gas at room temperature is a nonmetal
checks.note: Metals are solid 'with the exception of mercury' (Grokipedia Metal); 'all commonly recognized metalloids exist as solids' (Grokipedia Metalloid). Edge case only: the superheavy copernicium and flerovium are predicted volatile metals (flerovium perhaps liquid), but only single atoms have ever been made, so no bulk counterexample exists.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: a metal; a metalloid; a rare earth element
checks.note: No metal or metalloid is a gas at room temperature; the rare earths are all metals (Grokipedia Rare-earth_element: 'seventeen chemically similar metallic elements').

checks.claim: Context: hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, chlorine and the six noble gases such as helium and neon
checks.note: Grokipedia lists 'the six noble gases' among the 17 nonmetals (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn; oganesson is outside the count and is predicted to be a solid).

checks.claim: Context: all metals are solid at room temperature except mercury, a liquid; metalloids are all solids
checks.note: Mercury is 'the only metal liquid at room temperature' (melting point -38.8 C). Gallium (29.8 C) and caesium (28.5 C) melt just above ordinary room temperature, so the statement holds.

checks.claim: Context: carbon, sulfur and iodine are solids, bromine a liquid
checks.note: 'bromine (Br) is the sole liquid'; carbon, phosphorus, sulfur, selenium and iodine are the five solids.

checks.claim: Stem description fits sulfur: pale yellow, no metallic shine, crumbles when struck, almost no electricity passes
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a pale yellow, crystalline solid', 'odorless, tasteless, and brittle', 'poor electrical conductivity as a nonmetal solid'. Wikipedia Sulfur: 'all of the stable allotropes are excellent electrical insulators'.

checks.claim: Key: it sits on the right side of the table
checks.note: Sulfur is a nonmetal in group 16 (the chalcogens), on the right; nonmetals occupy 'the right-hand side of the periodic table' (Wikipedia Nonmetal).

checks.claim: Wrong choices: left side; across the middle
checks.note: Left and middle hold the metals, which are shiny, malleable and conduct.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: along the staircase line
checks.note: Metalloids 'generally appear metallic in luster'; the stem's 'no metallic shine' rules them out. (Yellow arsenic, an unstable allotrope, is far beyond the grade and does not make this choice defensible.)

checks.claim: Context: solid nonmetals are brittle and carry heat and electricity poorly
checks.note: The grade-level rule as Grokipedia states it ('brittleness in solid form', 'poor conductors of heat and electricity'). Known exceptions the writer's own sheet records (F16): graphite conducts electricity, diamond conducts heat very well, selenium can be drawn into wire. Optional: 'Most solid nonmetals are brittle...' since the pencil-graphite circuit is a common classroom demo.

checks.claim: Context: metalloids along the staircase are brittle too but shine like metals
checks.note: 'shiny, brittle solids'.

checks.claim: Key: silicon can be made to let electricity pass or stop it (a semiconductor)
checks.note: Grokipedia: conductivity 'between that of a conductor and an insulator'; doping adds trace elements to change it; 'conductivity can be switched on or off'. On the brief's question of whether the reason is right: being a semiconductor is why chips are made of one; silicon's edge over other semiconductors such as germanium is that it 'dominates due to its abundance, thermal stability, and ease of fabrication' (Grokipedia). The key gives the right, if partial, reason, and no wrong choice states the other part.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: lets electricity through more easily than copper
checks.note: Copper 5.96e7 S/m against silicon 4.35e-4 S/m at 20 C.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: blocks all electricity, the way glass does
checks.note: Glass 1e-15 to 1e-11 S/m; silicon is millions to billions of times more conductive.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: can be drawn into long thin wires
checks.note: Silicon 'is hard and brittle', not ductile.

checks.claim: Stem: chips built on thin slices of silicon; silicon is a metalloid
checks.note: Silicon 'is the foundation of the semiconductor industry, enabling transistors, microchips'; listed among the six metalloids.

checks.claim: Context: far less easily than copper, far more easily than glass; doping changes how much it carries
checks.note: Figures above; doping per Grokipedia Semiconductor.

checks.claim: Context: a chip holds billions of tiny silicon switches called transistors
checks.note: A transistor 'functions as an amplifier or electronic switch'; 'the most common material is silicon'; modern phones hold 'billions of transistors'. True of the processor and memory chips meant here, not of every small chip; optional: 'A modern processor chip holds billions...'.

checks.claim: Context: silicon is brittle, so it cannot be drawn into wire as copper can
Key: the neodymium part is a magnet
checks.note: Neodymium magnets are used in 'Drive motors for hybrid and electric vehicles', wind turbine generators 'with permanent magnet excitation', and 'Loudspeakers and headphones'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: wire coil, microchip, switch
checks.note: Coils are copper, chips silicon; neodymium's use in these devices is the magnet.

checks.claim: Stem: neodymium is one of the rare earth elements
checks.note: A lanthanide (element 60), one of the 17.

checks.claim: Stem: 'Electric car motors ... all hold a part made with neodymium' (unqualified)
checks.note: Minor overstatement. Permanent-magnet motors are about 84-86% of the electric car market (IDTechEx, 2021-22); the rest are magnet-free induction motors (Tesla) or wound-rotor motors (Renault, BMW's 5th-generation drive). The writer already hedged 'many wind turbines' (Wikipedia: most wind turbines do not use permanent magnets) but not the car motors. Fix: 'Most electric car motors, the generators in many wind turbines and the speakers in most headphones all hold a part made with neodymium...'. The key and choices are unaffected.

checks.claim: Context: neodymium with iron and boron makes the strongest permanent magnets sold
checks.note: 'an alloy of neodymium, iron, and boron'; 'the strongest type of permanent magnet available commercially'.

checks.claim: Context: the 17 rare earth elements are all metals
checks.note: 'a group of seventeen chemically similar metallic elements': the 15 lanthanides plus scandium and yttrium.

checks.claim: Context: not scarce in Earth's crust; spread thinly through rock, seldom gathered in one place
checks.note: USGS: 'not rare in terms of average crustal abundance, but the concentrated deposits ... are limited in number'; Grokipedia: 'not scarce in the Earth's crust', 'rarely form concentrated deposits'. One exception a reader might raise: promethium, radioactive with no stable isotope, exists in nature only in traces (a few hundred grams in the whole crust); harmless at this grade.

unit_notes: Fact-checked 2026-11-26, Grokipedia first, Wikipedia, USGS, etymonline and others second. 7 ok, 1 error (minor: the neodymium stem's unqualified 'Electric car motors'; add 'Most'). Optional polish, not errors: Q1's context gives Grokipedia's reading of Berzelius's aim (Latin 'to ensure consistency across languages'), which his own words do not state; Q6's context could say 'Most solid nonmetals' (graphite conducts); Q7's context could say 'A modern processor chip'. Room-temperature state claims (11 gases, mercury the only liquid metal) hold for every element made in bulk; the superheavy copernicium and flerovium are only predicted volatile metals.
